To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TK(-) mutants of herpes simplex virus type 1 can reactivate from latency in mouse trigemina ganglia if TK(+) virus is present in the co-inoculum.

TK(-) and TK(+) herpes simplex virus can co-infect mouse trigeminal neurons, and that the replication, number and reactivation efficiency in trigeminal neurons of TK(+) viruses are reduced in a manner proportional to the amount of the TK(-) virus present.

TK(-) virus can reduce the replication of co-infecting TK(+) virus during acute infection of mouse ganglia and that co-infecting, complementing TK(+) viruses can increase the number of viral genomes and reactivating TK(-) mutants in latently infected mouse ganglia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the presence of TK(-) mutants affects the ability of a co-infecting TK(+) virus to establish a persistent infection and reactivate from latency in mouse trigemimal ganglia.
the role of TK(+) and TK(-) viruses in mixed infections of mouse ganglia.
the interaction of TK(-) and TK(+) viruses during the establishment and maintenance of HSV latency and reactivation in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TK(-) and TK(+) viruses can co-infect mouse ganglia, but the replication, number and pathogenic potential of TK(+) viruses are diminished in the presence of TK(-) viruses.
the replication of TK(+) and TK(-) viruses is not independent in mouse ganglia, but that the two types of viruses can interact to produce a pathogenic phenotype.
the replication of TK(+) and TK(-) viruses is competitive and complementary in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
co-infection with wild-type virus can complement the acute replication and latency of a TK(-) virus.
the replication of TK(-) mutants in mouse ganglia is not always complemented by co-infection with wild-type virus, but the pathogenic phenotype can be conferred in the absence of complementation.
TK(-) virus can inhibit the acute replication, number of latently infected neurons and reactivation efficiency, but not always the latent genome copy numbers of co-infecting TK(+) virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of TK(-) viruses in the inoculum can significantly reduce the replication and latency of TK(+) viruses in mouse ganglia.
TK(-) and TK(+) viruses are not always mutually exclusive in vivo and can interact in complex ways that depend on the relative amounts and ratios of the two types of virus.
TK(-) and TK(+) viruses compete with one another in mouse ganglia during acute infection and that TK(-) mutants are not always complemented in vivo by TK(+) virus.
